summary.text: A posterior probability is a conditional probability found by updating a prior probability with the evidence, using Bayes' rule.
It is proportional to the product Likelihood · Prior probability.
Once new information arrives, the current posterior can serve as the prior in another round of Bayesian updating.

facts.label: Reused as
facts.value: The prior in the next round of updating

facts.label: Practical catch
facts.value: Generally not tractable, so it must be approximated

facts.label: Trousers example
facts.value: Seeing trousers gives a 25% chance the student is a girl

items.prompt: A school has 60% boys and 40% girls. All boys wear trousers, and girls wear trousers or skirts in equal numbers. You glimpse a random student in trousers. How likely is it to be a girl?

options.label: 40%, her share of the school
50%, since girls split evenly
60%, since trousers are common
25%, a quarter of trouser wearers

items.explain: Among N students, boys are 0.6N and girls 0.4N, so girls among trouser wearers are (50% of 0.4N)/(0.6N + 50% of 0.4N) = 25%.

items.prompt: You finish one round of updating, then a second batch of data arrives. What do you use as the starting point for the new round?

options.label: The original starting assumption, unchanged
A blank assumption that treats all outcomes alike
Only the second batch of data on its own
The posterior from the first round

items.explain: After new information arrives, the current posterior probability may serve as the prior in another round of Bayesian updating.

items.prompt: A school is 40% girls. You glimpse a random student in trousers and your estimate that she is a girl goes down. Why?

options.label: Trousers are more common among boys than girls here
Girls never wear trousers in this school
Seeing any student lowers every estimate
The observer simply gets tired and guesses

items.explain: All boys wear trousers but only half the girls do, so seeing trousers points toward a boy and the chance she is a girl falls from 40% to 25%.

items.prompt: The posterior probability is proportional to the product of which two things?

options.label: The prior and the sample size
The likelihood and the prior
The mean and the variance
The evidence and its opposite

items.explain: The posterior probability is proportional to the product Likelihood · Prior probability.

items.prompt: The idea of a posterior distribution is simple, yet people often reach for numerical methods to get it. Why?

options.label: It always comes out as a single whole number
It can only be found by asking an expert
It is generally not tractable, so it must be approximated
It cannot be computed once data is observed

items.explain: While conceptually simple, the posterior distribution is generally not tractable, so it has to be approximated analytically or numerically.

items.prompt: You want to show how uncertain a posterior probability is. Which summary does the idea offer?

options.label: A credible interval
A single guess with no range
The prior with the data removed
A count of how many data points exist

items.explain: Because the posterior is conditioned on random data, it helps to summarize its uncertainty, and one way is to provide a credible interval.
